Name: Garum Fish-Sauce Fermentation Workshops and the Salty Flow of Mediterranean Gold
RagShortTexts: Large stone garum fermentation vats were built all along the Mediterranean coast, where mackerel guts were salted and left in the sun
The savory liquid, rich in glutamate, was poured into two-handled pointed amphorae and sold widely in Rome and in army camps
Gadir and Malaca on the southern coast of Iberia were centers of top-grade fish sauce and monopolized its trade and profits
BaseText: 'Garum' (or Liquamen) was the irreplaceable soul of flavor and a pillar of bulk trade in the classical Mediterranean world. At Gadir, New Carthage and along the coast of southern Italy stood many orderly open-air workshops of large, watertight plastered stone vats. Workers layered the guts, gills and scraps of great quantities of freshly caught mackerel, sardines and tuna with highly concentrated sea salt, added herbs such as oregano and coriander, and left them to ferment under the fierce summer sun for two to three months. Once the fish proteins had been completely broken down and liquefied by their own enzymes, craftsmen pressed tightly woven reed baskets into the vats, and the clear, amber liquid that seeped into the baskets was the finest garum. This liquid was intensely savory; it was poured into specially made two-handled pointed amphorae (Amphora) and shipped everywhere with the grain fleets. It was both an indispensable dipping sauce at the banquets of Roman nobles and a life-saving ration that supplied the salt and protein legionaries needed for long marches.

Variants.Content: A dish without garum is like Italy without sunshine! Just a few drops of New Carthage fish sauce in a bitter soup of roasted lentils, and it turns at once into a delicacy fit for the gods!

Mackerel from the sea plus the blazing sun of Andalusia is worth more than a gold mine! Even while the two sides' warships turn the sea upside down, amphorae full of garum still fetch heavy silver coins in the ports on both shores.

That pungent, fermented, salty-fishy smell makes you retch at first, but after you have gnawed on dry, hard wheat biscuit for two months, one mouthful of hard bread with garum lets you carry your heavy shield another thirty miles.
